The image shows an opened abdominal cavity heavily infiltrated with widespread, multinodular tumor growth. This appearance is highly characteristic of **peritoneal carcinomatosis**.

### What is Peritoneal Carcinomatosis?

Peritoneal carcinomatosis occurs when a primary cancer (often from the ovary, colon, stomach, or pancreas) spreads (metastasizes) to the peritoneum, which is the thin membrane lining the abdominal cavity and covering the abdominal organs.

Instead of spreading only through the bloodstream or lymphatic system, cancer cells "seed" the peritoneal cavity. They break away from the original tumor and travel through the peritoneal fluid, implanting themselves across the surfaces of the abdominal wall and the organs within. This results in the appearance of numerous nodules—ranging from tiny, millet-seed-sized spots to large, coalescing masses—as seen in this image.

### Diagnosis

While the gross appearance is very suggestive of peritoneal carcinomatosis, a definitive diagnosis and identification of the primary source of the cancer require a histopathological examination. A pathologist would take samples (biopsies) of these nodules and examine them under a microscope to determine the specific type of malignant cells involved.<turn|>
